title: A right ventricle that will not cooperate
subtitle: A 55-year-old man on postoperative day 1 after durable LVAD implantation, with rising CVP, falling pump flow, and a lactate that will not clear.
objectives: Recognize early RV failure after durable LVAD implantation from the combination of CVP, PA pulsatility, septal position, and LVAD parameters, and explain why increasing pump speed makes it worse.
Describe the RV-LVAD interaction: how LV unloading changes RV preload, septal geometry, and afterload, and why a borderline RV declares itself in the first 48 hours.
Compare a percutaneous dual-lumen RA-to-PA cannula with a centrifugal pump, a surgical temporary RVAD, and VA ECMO for RV support after LVAD, in a patient with a fresh sternotomy and a running LVAD.

Explain what the oxygenator in the RA-to-PA circuit does, how to prove it is no longer needed, and what its removal involves. Distinguish the same cannula's use as a single-cannula VV ECMO configuration from its use as an RVAD.
Design a weaning trial for a temporary RVAD running against a durable LVAD, name the data that permit decannulation, and describe the failure modes to watch for.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 55-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and INTERMACS profile 3 underwent HeartMate 3 implantation yesterday as bridge to candidacy. Preoperative right heart catheterization showed a moderately elevated PA pressure with a preserved transpulmonary gradient, an RA pressure in the low teens, and a PA pulsatility index that the heart failure team described as borderline. Preoperative TTE showed moderately reduced RV function and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. He came off bypass on inhaled nitric oxide at 40 ppm, epinephrine at 2 mcg/min, and milrinone at 0.125 mcg/kg/min, and arrived in the CTICU on the same support. The surgeon's note describes a straightforward implant with no RV concerns at chest closure. [REVIEW]

It is now 06:00 on postoperative day 1. Overnight the CVP has climbed from the low teens into the low 20s. The PA catheter shows a pulmonary artery pressure that has become less pulsatile, with a narrowing difference between systolic and diastolic PA pressure. Mixed venous saturation has fallen into the low 50s. Lactate has risen through the night and is not clearing. Urine output has tapered. [REVIEW]

The LVAD controller shows: speed unchanged from the operating room, estimated flow lower than at ICU arrival, pulsatility index lower than at arrival, power stable. There have been two low-flow events overnight. Per the unit's usual sequence, the nitric oxide wean began at 22:00 and had reached 20 ppm by 02:00, with the CVP drifting up through that period. The overnight resident increased the speed by a small increment at 03:00 in response to the low flow, after which the flow improved briefly and then fell again. The nitric oxide is still at 20 ppm. [REVIEW]

Chest tubes have drained moderately with no acute change. The mediastinal drains are not clotted. He is intubated and sedated, on a lung-protective ventilator strategy with moderate PEEP. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: What is happening to this patient, and what would you do first? Be explicit about what the nitric oxide wean and the speed increase at 03:00 each did, and why. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is early RV failure after LVAD implantation. The pattern is the classic one: rising CVP, loss of PA pulsatility, falling mixed venous saturation and rising lactate, and an LVAD that reports low flow and low pulsatility. The LVAD is not failing. It is starved. A continuous-flow LVAD can only pump what the RV delivers across the pulmonary circulation into the LV. When the RV cannot fill the LV, the pump draws the LV cavity down, the septum shifts toward the inflow cannula, and the flow estimate falls. [REVIEW]

The RV-LVAD interaction has three elements the fellow should be able to recite:

- **Preload.** LV unloading increases venous return and cardiac output demand on an RV that was already marginal. The RV is asked to deliver the whole of the LVAD's flow, which is often more than it delivered before implant.
- **Septal geometry.** The interventricular septum contributes substantially to RV ejection. When the LVAD empties the LV and the septum shifts leftward, that contribution is lost and the RV becomes a dilated, poorly contracting, geometrically disadvantaged chamber. Tricuspid regurgitation worsens as the annulus dilates.
- **Afterload.** LVAD support lowers left atrial pressure and should lower pulmonary venous congestion over days, but on the first night the pulmonary vascular resistance is often higher than preoperatively because of bypass, transfusion, hypoxemia, acidosis, and protamine. The RV sees high afterload and high preload at the same time. [REVIEW]

**What the nitric oxide wean did.** It was routine, and in a patient with a competent RV it would have been uneventful. Here it removed pulmonary vasodilation from an RV that was already working against a postoperative rise in pulmonary vascular resistance, and the CVP started climbing as the dose came down. Nitric oxide weaning also carries a rebound risk of its own, with pulmonary vascular resistance overshooting the pre-treatment level as endogenous nitric oxide synthase recovers from suppression, which is why the unit weans in steps rather than stopping. The lesson is that a standard wean is a test of the RV, and the test was failed. The first drug change is to return the nitric oxide to 40 ppm and stop weaning.

**What the 03:00 speed increase did.** It was the intuitive response to a low-flow reading and it was the wrong one. Raising speed on a starved pump increases the suction on an LV that is already empty, pulls the septum further toward the inflow cannula, worsens RV geometry and tricuspid regurgitation, and can trigger suction events. The brief improvement in flow was the pump transiently drawing down residual LV volume. The subsequent fall is the RV failing to refill it. The trap is that the controller displays an LV-side number for an RV-side problem. The correct response to low flow with a high CVP is to look at the RV, not to turn up the LVAD. [REVIEW]

**First actions, in order.** Bedside echo now to confirm the picture (dilated RV, leftward septal shift, small LV with the inflow cannula close to the septum or free wall, severe tricuspid regurgitation, no tamponade). Exclude tamponade specifically: a fresh sternotomy with a rising CVP and falling flow is tamponade until the echo says otherwise, and loculated posterior collections are easy to miss on TTE, so TEE or a low threshold for surgical re-exploration is appropriate. [REVIEW] Then reduce the LVAD speed back toward the baseline that allowed the septum to sit midline, correct the drivers of pulmonary vascular resistance (oxygenation, pH, PCO2, PEEP, pain, agitation), and escalate RV support on the agents he is already receiving. Return the nitric oxide to 40 ppm and confirm the circuit is intact and the cylinder is not depleted. Increase the epinephrine, in steps of 1 to 2 mcg/min, for contractility. Increase the milrinone to 0.25 mcg/kg/min for inodilation and pulmonary vasodilation, accepting that it will lower systemic vascular resistance and that a MAP falling below the coronary perfusion pressure the RV needs is itself an RV insult. If the MAP drops with the milrinone, add vasopressin rather than more epinephrine, since vasopressin supports systemic pressure with little effect on pulmonary vascular resistance. The order matters: nitric oxide and speed reduction act on the problem (afterload and geometry), inotropes act on the compensation, and both are a bridge to the decision about mechanical RV support, not a substitute for it.

What should not be done: a large fluid bolus. A CVP in the 20s with a dilated RV is a volume-overloaded RV, and more volume worsens the septal shift that is starving the LVAD.

questions.prompt: Which single LVAD parameter change would you expect to be the earliest and most specific bedside signal of RV failure on a continuous-flow LVAD? Why do the other candidates fall short?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: A fall in pulsatility index, together with the clinical picture.** Pulsatility index on a continuous-flow LVAD reflects the contribution of native LV contraction to flow through the pump, which in turn depends on LV filling. When the RV fails and the LV empties, pulsatility falls. It falls before the flow estimate becomes alarming, and it falls in the direction opposite to what LV recovery or hypertension would produce. It is not specific on its own (hypovolemia, tamponade, and arrhythmia also lower it), which is why it must be read with the CVP and the echo. [REVIEW]

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **Estimated flow.** It is a calculation from speed and power, not a measurement, and it is what the resident reacted to overnight. It falls late and it falls for many reasons. The manufacturer's documentation is explicit that flow is an estimate. [VERIFY]
- **Power.** Power rises with pump thrombosis and with higher speed and falls with obstruction. It is stable in this patient because the pump is not the problem. A stable power with falling flow is itself informative: it argues against thrombus and toward a preload problem.
- **Speed.** Speed is a setting, not a signal. It only changes when someone changes it.

The larger point is that no LVAD parameter is an RV monitor. The RV monitors are the CVP, the PA pulsatility, the mixed venous saturation, the lactate, and the echo. The pump parameters tell you the LV is empty. The patient tells you why.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
Twelve hours later. TEE confirmed a dilated, severely hypokinetic RV, severe tricuspid regurgitation, a leftward septum, and a small LV with the inflow cannula directed toward the septum. There was no pericardial collection. Speed was reduced to a level at which the septum sat closer to midline and suction events stopped. He is now on epinephrine at 8 mcg/min, milrinone at 0.375 mcg/kg/min, inhaled nitric oxide at 40 ppm, and vasopressin at 0.04 units/min for a MAP that drifted down with the milrinone. Ventilation has been optimized. [REVIEW]

Despite this, CVP remains in the 20s, lactate continues to rise, urine output has stopped, and the LVAD flow estimate is lower than it was this morning. Mixed venous saturation is in the mid 40s. The arterial PaO2 is adequate on FiO2 0.6. Creatinine has doubled since the morning and the potassium is climbing. Nephrology has been consulted, a dialysis catheter has been placed in the left femoral vein, and CVVH has started with a slow net negative fluid goal. [REVIEW]

The surgical and heart failure attendings are at the bedside. The options on the table are a percutaneous dual-lumen RA-to-PA cannula (ProtekDuo) with an external centrifugal pump, a surgical temporary RVAD placed through the sternotomy (RA drainage, PA graft return), or peripheral VA ECMO. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Maximal medical RV support has failed. Compare the three mechanical options for this specific patient, with an LVAD running and a sternotomy closed yesterday, and commit to one. Say what each option does to the LVAD.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer in this patient: a percutaneous RA-to-PA RVAD, a ProtekDuo cannula via the right internal jugular vein with an external centrifugal pump, configured with an oxygenator in the circuit from the start.** At Northwestern the ProtekDuo circuit is built with the oxygenator in line and the oxygenator is removed once gas exchange allows, rather than added later when it fails. Splicing an oxygenator into a running circuit is a planned interruption of RV support with a clamped line and an air risk, and the lungs after bypass, transfusion, and a night of congestion rarely stay adequate. Starting with it in costs some flow resistance and anticoagulation exposure. Starting without it bets the lungs. The reasoning is about what each option does to the LVAD and to the chest. [REVIEW]

- **Percutaneous RA-to-PA RVAD.** Drains the RA through the proximal lumen and returns blood to the main PA through the distal lumen, which sits across the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. The RV is bypassed. The LV is filled by the pump at a controllable flow, which means the LVAD once again has something to pump and its parameters become interpretable. Pulmonary blood flow is antegrade and physiologic. The chest is not reopened. The device is a 29 Fr or 31 Fr dual-lumen cannula placed via the right IJ, typically under fluoroscopy with TEE, and published series report flows up to roughly 4 L/min. [VERIFY] Limitations: it requires a right IJ that can accept a large cannula, PA tip position must be confirmed and can migrate, flow is bounded by the cannula, and it needs a team that places and manages it regularly. In patients with an existing LVAD, Coromilas and colleagues reported that percutaneous RVAD support was feasible with outcomes comparable to surgical RVAD in a single-center series, with the advantage of avoiding re-sternotomy. [REVIEW]
- **Surgical temporary RVAD.** Larger cannulas and higher achievable flow, direct PA return through a graft, and the option to deal with the tricuspid valve or bleeding at the same time. The cost is reopening a day-old sternotomy, with the bleeding, infection, and later re-closure that implies, plus a second trip to the operating room for removal. This is the better choice when flow requirements exceed what a percutaneous cannula provides, when the IJ is unusable, or when the chest needs to be reopened anyway for a surgical problem. [REVIEW]
- **Peripheral VA ECMO.** Provides biventricular support and oxygenation without opening the chest, and it is fast. But it is the wrong physiology for a patient with an LVAD in place. Retrograde femoral return raises afterload on an LVAD outflow graft and competes with it. The LVAD may need to be slowed to near-idle to avoid LV suck-down with no RV delivery and no antegrade pulmonary flow, which risks stasis in the LV, the inflow cannula, and the aortic root. Pulmonary blood flow falls, which worsens the lungs. The two devices fight. It is reasonable as a rescue when the patient is arresting or the other options are not available within minutes, and some centers use it as a bridge to a configured RVAD, but it is a poor steady-state solution. [REVIEW]

The dominant argument against VA ECMO here is that the patient has adequate oxygenation and a working LVAD. What he lacks is RV output. An RA-to-PA RVAD replaces precisely the missing function, keeps the lungs perfused antegrade, and keeps the LVAD doing its job.

What changes the answer: a surgical bleeding problem that needs the chest open regardless (favors surgical RVAD), or hemodynamic collapse (favors whatever can be placed fastest). At Northwestern, cardiac surgery places all of these: the ProtekDuo, the surgical RVAD, and peripheral VA ECMO cannulas. The ICU team's job is to make the case for which one, and to have the patient ready for whichever is chosen.

**The dialysis catheter.** The CVVH access went in the left femoral vein, not the right internal jugular, and that was not an accident. The right IJ is the route for the ProtekDuo and must be kept clean and uncannulated when mechanical RV support is on the table. Any line placed in a patient who might need percutaneous RV support should be sited with that in mind. Slow ultrafiltration on CVVH is also the right way to unload this RV. It reduces preload without the hemodynamic swing of a bolus diuretic in a patient whose kidneys have already stopped, and it moves the septum in the right direction. It is not a substitute for the RVAD. A CVP in the 20s with a lactate still rising is a flow problem, and ultrafiltration treats congestion, not output.

Cannula positioning: the proximal drainage ports sit in the RA and the distal return tip in the main PA beyond the pulmonic valve. Position is confirmed on fluoroscopy and TEE at placement and rechecked when flow becomes erratic. The manufacturer's instructions for use govern the specifics and should be the reference. [VERIFY]

stages.title: Taking the oxygenator out
stages.narrative:
Cardiac surgery placed the ProtekDuo via the right IJ under fluoroscopy and TEE, with the oxygenator in line from the start. Flow was set to a level at which the septum returned to midline and the LVAD flow estimate rose to a satisfactory value. CVP fell into the low teens. Lactate cleared overnight. Epinephrine is down to 4 mcg/min, milrinone to 0.25 mcg/kg/min, the nitric oxide is at 20 ppm, and the vasopressin is off. CVVH continues with a net negative goal of 100 mL/h. He remains about 6 L positive since surgery. [REVIEW]

Postoperative day 5. The lungs have recovered. He is on FiO2 0.4 and PEEP 8 with an adequate PaO2 and a clearing chest radiograph, and the sweep gas has already been turned down to 1 L/min. Over the past 24 hours perfusion has reported increasing fibrin at the oxygenator inlet, a rising transmembrane pressure gradient, a post-oxygenator PaO2 that has fallen from its earlier value, and a platelet count drifting down with a heparin infusion at the usual circuit target. [REVIEW]

The RV is not ready. A brief flow turn-down yesterday to 2 L/min produced a CVP rise into the high teens and a fall in LVAD pulsatility within ten minutes, and flow was returned to baseline. [REVIEW]

The perfusionist asks whether the oxygenator should come out of the circuit.

questions.prompt: Should the oxygenator come out now? Say how you would prove it is no longer needed, what removing it involves, what the circuit becomes afterward, and what you risk by leaving it in. Then address the configuration itself: a ProtekDuo with an oxygenator is also used as a single-cannula VV ECMO for respiratory failure. Is it an RVAD, a VV circuit, or both, and what does the answer imply for recirculation, PA pressure, and RV rest?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Yes, take it out, and do it as a planned procedure rather than waiting for it to fail.** The oxygenator was the right thing to start with and is now a liability. A membrane with visible fibrin, a rising transmembrane gradient, and a falling post-oxygenator PaO2 is clotting. Everything downstream of it goes straight into the pulmonary artery, so the lungs that have just recovered are the first organ to receive whatever it sheds. The falling platelet count is the consumptive signal of the same process. A clotting membrane also raises circuit resistance, and the flow it eventually costs is flow the RV still needs. The alternative, exchanging the oxygenator for a new one, buys a component the patient no longer requires at the price of the same circuit interruption. [REVIEW]

**Proving it is not needed.** Turning the FiO2 on the sweep gas down proves nothing while the sweep is still running, because the membrane still removes CO2 and still contributes oxygen at the blended fraction. The trial is a sweep-off trial: cap the sweep gas to zero with pump flow unchanged, leave the ventilator where it is, and draw an arterial gas at 30 to 60 minutes. The lungs now oxygenate and ventilate the entire pump output plus the native RV output, which is exactly the condition they will face after removal. Acceptable PaO2 and PaCO2 on FiO2 of 0.5 or less and PEEP of 10 or less, without a rise in minute ventilation demand, is a pass. Blood continues to flow through the membrane during the trial, so stasis is not added, but the trial should be short because a clotting oxygenator with no sweep is not improving. [REVIEW]

**Removal.** At Northwestern this is cardiac surgery and perfusion at the bedside. The oxygenator is clamped out and the tubing spliced and de-aired, which means a brief interruption of RV support in a patient whose RV failed a 2 L/min turn-down yesterday. Prepare for it the way you would prepare for the turn-down: a step up on the epinephrine beforehand, the nitric oxide confirmed on, volume at hand, the LVAD low-flow and suction alarms expected, and the attending in the room. The anticoagulation target may change once the membrane is gone, and the circuit surveillance that was built around the oxygenator (pre- and post-membrane gases, transmembrane gradient) stops. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**What the circuit becomes.** A plain RA-to-PA RVAD. The pump drains the RA and returns venous blood to the PA, and the lungs oxygenate all of it. The pre-pump saturation is now the mixed venous saturation and is the perfusion marker to follow. The RV support is unchanged. What has changed is that any new lung problem from here is a lung problem with no backup, so the ventilator strategy stays lung-protective and the threshold for re-imaging is low. [REVIEW]

**What you risk by leaving it in.** Embolization into the lungs, continued platelet consumption, a membrane that fails abruptly rather than gracefully, and a day when the oxygenator is exchanged under duress rather than removed with the team assembled.

**The naming question.** The same dual-lumen cannula, with an oxygenator and a centrifugal pump, drains the RA and returns oxygenated blood to the PA. That is exactly the configuration used as a single-cannula venovenous ECMO for respiratory failure, described in a series of COVID-19 ARDS cohorts and in lung transplant bridging, where it has been called V-P (veno-pulmonary) ECMO. Whether you call it Oxy-RVAD or V-P ECMO depends on which problem you were trying to solve when you built it. The physics is identical. The honest answer is that it is both: it is a VV circuit with respect to gas exchange, and it is an RVAD with respect to the RV, because the return limb sits beyond the pulmonic valve and the RV is bypassed at pump flow. [REVIEW]

**Recirculation.** Conventional dual-site VV ECMO returns oxygenated blood to the RA, where a fraction is drawn straight back into the drainage cannula. In the RA-to-PA configuration the drainage ports and the return tip are separated by the tricuspid and pulmonic valves, so recirculation is largely prevented. The systematic reviews by Maybauer, Capoccia, and colleagues make this point. The practical consequence is that the pre-oxygenator saturation on this circuit is a real mixed venous value and can be trusted as a perfusion marker, which is not true of a femoro-jugular VV circuit. [REVIEW]

**PA pressure.** The return limb delivers pump flow directly into the main PA. If the pulmonary vascular resistance is high and the pump flow is high, PA pressure will rise and the lungs can be injured by flow. The PA catheter tip, if one is in place alongside the cannula, needs to be distal to the return jet to read anything meaningful, and the tracing should be examined for the pump's contribution. Some operators place a PA catheter alongside. Whether this is done at NMH, and how PA pressure targets are set on this circuit, are institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**RV rest.** This is where the controversy lives. Proponents describe the configuration as resting the RV because the RV is bypassed. Skeptics point out that the RV still receives whatever venous return the cannula does not capture, that the RV is still exposed to PA pressure (now including the pump's contribution), and that an RV bypassed at 3 to 4 L/min of a 6 L/min venous return is only partially unloaded. The RV also loses the preload it would need to generate any output of its own, so the echo appearance of a quiet RV on support does not predict what it will do when flow is reduced. Both views are defensible. For this patient, whose problem began as RV failure, the RV support is the point and the oxygenator is the add-on. For a pure ARDS patient with a healthy RV, the same cannula provides a VV circuit whose RV effect is incidental and possibly unnecessary. [REVIEW]

The teaching distinction: configuration describes plumbing. Indication describes intent. The fellow should be able to name both for any circuit in the unit.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
Postoperative day 9. The lungs have recovered. The oxygenator was removed from the circuit on day 5 and oxygenation has remained adequate on modest ventilator settings since. He has been extubated. Inotropes are at low dose. CVP is in the high single digits. Lactate is normal. Echo this morning, at full RVAD flow, shows an RV that is still dilated but with visibly better free-wall motion than on day 1, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, a midline septum, and an LV that fills the inflow cannula well. The LVAD parameters have been stable for three days. [REVIEW]

The heart failure attending asks you to run a weaning assessment today.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would wean a temporary RA-to-PA RVAD that is running against a durable LVAD. Name the data you need at each step, the finding that stops the trial, and what makes the LVAD different from the usual RVAD wean.
questions.modelAnswer:
The wean is a stepwise flow reduction trial under continuous echo and PA catheter monitoring, with the LVAD speed held constant, and with the question at each step being a single one: can the native RV deliver enough flow to fill the LVAD? [REVIEW]

**Setup.** TEE or a good TTE window, a PA catheter with CVP and PA pressure, mixed venous saturation, an arterial line, and the LVAD controller displayed. Inotropes at the dose you intend to send him home on, or close to it. Anticoagulation continued through the trial because low circuit flow increases thrombosis risk. Sedation light. A perfusionist at the pump. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Steps.** Reduce RVAD flow in increments and hold at each for long enough to see a steady state, typically on the order of ten to fifteen minutes, down to a minimum flow below which the circuit should not be left running because of stasis. The exact increments, hold times, and minimum flow are institution-specific and depend on the pump and cannula. [NMH protocol, insert] [VERIFY] At each step record:

- **CVP and PA pressure.** A rise in CVP of more than a modest amount, or loss of PA pulsatility, means the RV cannot take over the flow being removed.
- **RV size, free-wall motion, septal position, tricuspid regurgitation on echo.** The RV will dilate somewhat as it takes on volume. What matters is whether it dilates and keeps contracting, or dilates and stalls.
- **LVAD flow estimate and pulsatility index.** These should hold. A falling LVAD flow and pulsatility as RVAD flow comes down means the LV is emptying because the RV is not refilling it. This is the single most useful signal and it is unique to the LVAD patient.
- **Mixed venous saturation and lactate at the end.** The perfusion check.
- **Vasoactive requirement.** A trial that only succeeds on a large inotrope escalation has not succeeded.

**What stops the trial.** A rising CVP with a falling LVAD flow is the pattern that says stop, restore full RVAD flow, and reassess in 48 hours. A septum that shifts leftward on echo as RVAD flow falls is the same message in a different modality. [REVIEW]

**What makes the LVAD different.** In a patient with a native LV, a failing RVAD wean shows up as hypotension and a falling cardiac output. In a patient with an LVAD, the LVAD maintains systemic flow for a while by drawing down whatever the LV has, so the arterial pressure can look fine while the LV empties. The first signal of failure is the pump's own parameters and the echo, not the blood pressure. The fellow who weans an RVAD against an LVAD by watching the MAP will miss the failure until it is a suction event. The second difference is that the LVAD speed is a variable you control. If the RV is borderline, it is tempting to lower LVAD speed to reduce RV demand, and this can be reasonable, but it trades RV support for LV decongestion and the trade should be explicit. [REVIEW]

**If the trial passes.** Decannulation is usually at the bedside or in a procedural area with surgical backup, since the cannula crosses two valves and the PA. Hemostasis at the IJ, anticoagulation plan afterward, and the echo and PA catheter schedule for the next 72 hours are institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] After decannulation the risk does not end. Late RV failure after LVAD is a distinct entity with its own case elsewhere in this library.

**If it fails twice.** The conversation shifts to whether the RV will recover at all, which brings durable biventricular support or transplant listing into view. That is a heart failure team decision and the ICU's role is to keep him a candidate.

teachingPoints:
- A continuous-flow LVAD can only pump what the RV delivers. Low flow and low pulsatility with a high CVP is an RV problem displayed on an LV device. Turning up the speed makes it worse.
- The RV-LVAD interaction has three parts: higher preload demand, loss of septal contribution as the LV empties, and a transiently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance in the first 48 hours. Borderline RVs fail on the first night.
- Tamponade after a fresh sternotomy mimics RV failure on every monitor. Exclude it on echo before attributing the picture to the RV, and keep a low threshold for TEE.
- Pulsatility index is the earliest LVAD-side signal. Estimated flow is a calculation. Power is a pump-health signal, not a preload signal.
- For RV failure with a running LVAD and adequate oxygenation, an RA-to-PA RVAD replaces the missing function and keeps pulmonary flow antegrade. VA ECMO competes with the LVAD and is a rescue, not a plan.
- A ProtekDuo with an oxygenator is an Oxy-RVAD, which is the same plumbing as single-cannula V-P ECMO. Configuration describes plumbing. Indication describes intent. The oxygenator comes out when a sweep-off trial shows the lungs can handle the full pump output, and before the membrane fails.
- The RA-to-PA configuration largely avoids recirculation because two valves separate drainage from return, so the pre-oxygenator saturation is a trustworthy mixed venous value.
- Weaning an RVAD against an LVAD: the failure signal is a rising CVP with falling LVAD flow and a leftward septum, not the MAP. The LVAD will hide hemodynamic failure until it is a suction event.
pitfalls:
- Increasing LVAD speed in response to a low-flow alarm when the CVP is high.
- Giving volume to a CVP in the 20s with a dilated RV.
- Attributing the day-1 picture to RV failure without excluding tamponade, including loculated posterior collections that TTE misses.
- Choosing VA ECMO for a patient with an LVAD and adequate oxygenation because it is familiar and fast, and then spending days managing the competition between two pumps.
- Judging oxygenator readiness for removal by turning the sweep FiO2 down. Only a sweep-off trial proves the lungs can oxygenate and ventilate the entire pump output.
- Leaving a clotting oxygenator in a circuit that returns to the pulmonary artery. Everything it sheds goes to the lungs.
- Trusting a PA catheter tracing on an RA-to-PA circuit without knowing where the catheter tip sits relative to the return jet.
- Weaning the RVAD while watching the arterial pressure. The LVAD maintains MAP while the LV empties.
- Leaving a circuit at very low flow for a prolonged trial without attention to stasis and anticoagulation.
controversies:
**RVAD versus VA ECMO after LVAD.** There is no trial. Single-center series, including Coromilas and colleagues at Columbia, support percutaneous RVAD as feasible and comparable to surgical RVAD after durable LVAD. VA ECMO remains the fastest rescue and is used in some centers as a bridge to a configured RVAD. The physiologic argument against VA ECMO as a steady state with an LVAD in place (retrograde flow competing with the outflow graft, loss of antegrade pulmonary flow, stasis risk) is widely accepted but is reasoning, not evidence. [REVIEW]

**Prophylactic or planned RVAD at implant.** Some centers place a temporary RVAD at the time of LVAD implant in patients with high predicted RV failure risk, on the argument that planned support in the operating room beats emergency support on day 1. Others argue that RV failure risk scores perform poorly, that many high-risk RVs do fine, and that an unneeded RVAD adds bleeding, infection, and a second procedure. The 2023 ISHLT guideline discusses RV failure risk assessment and management but the decision for planned RVAD remains a judgment call. [REVIEW] [NMH protocol, insert]

**Timing of RVAD.** Earlier mechanical RV support is associated with better outcomes in observational series, but the series are confounded by selection. The honest statement is that an RV that is not improving on maximal medical therapy within hours, with rising lactate and failing end organs, should get a device before the kidneys and liver fail, and that waiting for a defined threshold has no evidence base. [REVIEW]

**Whether the V-P configuration offers RV support at all.** For a patient whose indication was ARDS, the RA-to-PA cannula is sometimes marketed and described as providing RV support in addition to gas exchange. The RV is bypassed at pump flow, which is real, but the RV still receives the uncaptured venous return and still faces PA pressure augmented by the pump. Whether the RV benefit is clinically meaningful in ARDS, versus simply being a recirculation-free VV configuration with a large single cannula, is unsettled and the systematic reviews are explicit that the evidence is limited and observational. [REVIEW]

**Weaning protocol.** Flow reduction trials are universal in principle and variable in every detail: increments, hold times, minimum flow, echo criteria, and what counts as an acceptable CVP rise. No consensus document specifies them for RA-to-PA devices. The protocol in this case is a structure, not a standard. [NMH protocol, insert]
discussWithAttending: The resident raised LVAD speed at 03:00 in response to a low-flow alarm. Describe the patient in whom that would have been the right move, and the single bedside finding that separates that patient from this one.
